edition.copy_text: Koetschau, GCS 2–3 (1899), via the Perseus TEI

source_text: Ἐπεὶ δὲ βούλεται Κέλσος κοινοποιεῖν τὰ σεμνὰ Ἰουδαίων ἐθνῶν τινων νόμοις. φέρε καὶ ταῦτα θεωρήσωμεν. νομίζει τοίνυν τὸ περὶ οὐρανοῦ δόγμα μηδὲν διαφέρειν τοῦ περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ καί φησι παραπλησίως τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις τοὺς Πέρσας τῷ Διῒ θυσίας ἐπιτελεῖν. ἐπὶ τὰ ὑψηλότατα τῶν ὀρέων ἀναβαίνοντας οὐχ ὁρῶν ὅτι Ἰουδαῖοι ὡς ἕνα θεὸν ἠπίσταντο. οὕτως ἕνα τὸν τῆς προσευχῆς ἅγιον οἶκον καὶ ἓν τὸ τῶν ὁλοκαρπωμάτων θυσιαστήριον καὶ ἓν τὸ τῶν θυμιαμάτων θυμιατήριον καὶ ἕνα τὸν τοῦ θεοῦ ἀρχιερέα. οὐδὲν οὖν κοινὸν πρὸς Πέρσας ἦν Ἰουδαίοις, ἐπὶ τὰ ὑψηλότατα τῶν ὀρέων, πλειόνων ὄντων, ἀναβαίνοντας καὶ θυσίας ἐπιτελοῦντας, οὐδὲν παραπλήσιον ἐχούσας ταῖς κατὰ τὸν Μωϋσέως νόμον· καθ᾿ ὃν „ὑποδείγματι καὶ σκιᾷ“ ἐλάτρευον „τῶν ἐπουρανίων“ οἱ Ἰουδαίων ἱερεῖς, ἐν ἀποῤῥήτῳ διηγούμενοι τὸ τοῦ νόμου περὶ τῶν θυσιῶν βούλημα καὶ ὧν σύμβολα ἦσαν αὗται. Πέρσαι τοίνυν πάντα τὸν τοῦ οὐρανοῦ κύκλον Δία καλείτωσαν, ἡμεῖς δὲ οὔτε Δία οὔτε τὸν θεόν φαμεν εἶναι τὸν οὐρανὸν, οἵ γε ἐπιστάμεθα καὶ τινα τῶν ἡττόνων τοῦ θεοῦ ὑπεραναβεβηκέναι τοὺς οὐρανοὺς καὶ πᾶσαν αἰσθητὴν φύσιν. καὶ οὕτω γε συνίεμεν τοῦ· „αἰνεῖτε τὸν θεὸν οἱ οὐρανοὶ τῶν οὐρανῶν, καὶ τὸ ὕδωρ τὸ ὑπεράνω τῶν οὐρανῶν· αἰνεσάτωσαν τὸ ὄνομα κυρίου.“
thought_title: One God, one temple, and the heaven of heavens
pass_a_gloss: Since Celsus wishes to make common (κοινοποιεῖν) the august things (τὰ σεμνά) of the Jews with the laws of certain nations, come, let us consider (θεωρήσωμεν) these things too. He thinks then that the doctrine about heaven differs nothing from that about God, and says that similarly (παραπλησίως) to the Jews the Persians accomplish (ἐπιτελεῖν) sacrifices to Zeus, going up onto the highest of the mountains; not seeing that the Jews, as they knew (ἠπίσταντο) one God, so [had] one the holy house (οἶκος) of prayer (προσευχή), and one the altar (θυσιαστήριον) of whole burnt offerings (ὁλοκαρπώματα), and one the incense-altar/censer (θυμιατήριον) of incense (θυμιάματα), and one the high priest (ἀρχιερεύς) of God. Nothing therefore in common was there for Jews towards Persians, going up onto the highest of the mountains, being many (πλειόνων), and accomplishing sacrifices having nothing similar to those according to the law of Moses; according to which [law] 'with a copy (ὑπόδειγμα) and shadow (σκιά)' the priests of the Jews served/worshipped (ἐλάτρευον) 'the heavenly things (τὰ ἐπουράνια)', in secret (ἐν ἀπορρήτῳ) expounding (διηγούμενοι) the intent (βούλημα) of the law about the sacrifices and of what things these were symbols. Let the Persians then call the whole circle of heaven Zeus; but we say neither Zeus nor God to be heaven, we who know that even someone of those lesser (ἡττόνων) than God has gone up beyond (ὑπεραναβεβηκέναι) the heavens and all sensible nature. And thus we understand (συνίεμεν) the [saying]: 'Praise (αἰνεῖτε) God, you heavens of the heavens, and the water above (ὑπεράνω) the heavens; let them praise the name of the Lord (κύριος).'

choices.why: αἰσθητὴ φύσις: 'sensible nature' -> 'nature that the senses perceive'
noted that τινα may be neuter plural ('some of the beings lower than God'); singular kept
Hebrews 8:5 verified; Psalm 148:4-5 verified (LXX and English numbering agree; Origen has τὸν θεόν for αὐτόν)

pass_b_english: Since Celsus wants to put the solemn institutions of the Jews on a level with the laws of certain nations, come, let us examine these points too. He thinks, then, that the doctrine about heaven is no different from the doctrine about God, and he says that the Persians, like the Jews, offer sacrifices to Zeus, going up to the highest peaks of the mountains. He does not see that, as the Jews knew one God, so they had one holy house of prayer, one altar for whole burnt offerings, one altar for incense, and one high priest of God.

The Jews, then, had nothing in common with the Persians, who go up to the highest peaks of the mountains, of which there are many, and offer sacrifices that bear no likeness to those under the law of Moses. Under that law the priests of the Jews served “a copy and shadow of the heavenly things” (Hebrews 8:5), and they explained in secret the intention of the law concerning the sacrifices, and of what things these sacrifices were symbols.

So let the Persians call the whole circle of heaven Zeus. We, however, say that heaven is neither Zeus nor God, since we know that even one of the beings lower than God has risen above the heavens and above the whole of nature that the senses perceive. And this is how we understand the words: “Praise God, you heavens of heavens, and the water that is above the heavens; let them praise the name of the Lord” (Psalm 148:4–5).
notes: The staged text has periods after νόμοις, after ἀναβαίνοντας and after ἠπίσταντο that split single sentences; they are read as one argument. θυμιατήριον can mean a censer or the altar of incense (cf. Hebrews 9:4); rendered 'one altar for incense' as the counterpart of the altar of burnt offering. The 'one house, one altar, one high priest' theme reflects the law of the single sanctuary (Deuteronomy 12:5-14) but quotes no verse, so it is not cited inline. 'ὑποδείγματι καὶ σκιᾷ λατρεύουσιν τῶν ἐπουρανίων' is Hebrews 8:5, adapted into past narrative (ἐλάτρευον). Psalm 148:4-5: LXX and English numbering agree for this psalm; the LXX reads αἰνεῖτε αὐτόν ('praise him'), and Origen substitutes τὸν θεόν; rendered as Origen has it. 'τινα τῶν ἡττόνων τοῦ θεοῦ ὑπεραναβεβηκέναι τοὺς οὐρανούς' is singular in the Greek ('someone of those lesser than God'); it probably refers to the soul of Jesus, recalling Hebrews 4:14 (διεληλυθότα τοὺς οὐρανούς) and Ephesians 4:10 (ὑπεράνω πάντων τῶν οὐρανῶν), but Origen does not quote either, so they are not cited inline. The singular τινα is kept: 'even one of the beings lower than God has risen'. Reviewer: unaccented τινα could also be neuter plural ('some of the beings lower than God have risen'), e.g. the souls of the saints; the Greek does not settle it, and the singular is kept as the likelier reading with Hebrews 4:14 in view. αἰσθητὴ φύσις rendered 'nature that the senses perceive', as in 5.42.

Open doubt (review): 5.44: unaccented τινα in 'τινα τῶν ἡττόνων τοῦ θεοῦ ὑπεραναβεβηκέναι τοὺς οὐρανούς' may be masculine singular (likely the soul of Jesus) or neuter plural (some lesser beings); singular kept and the ambiguity noted in translator_notes
